Using ggmtools with other methods

Source: vignettes/articles/other-methods.Rmd
other-methods.Rmd

ggmtools has two layers:

  • Generics (pip_table(), pcor_estimate()) that a package implements for its own fitted objects. spikeyglass and multiGGM provide methods, and ggmtools itself provides pcor_estimate() for JGL fits, so the same downstream code runs on fits from any of them.
  • Matrix-level functions for everything else: evaluation, losses, tuning, edge selection and edge tables. These take precision, partial-correlation, score or adjacency matrices, or vectors of probabilities and p-values, never a fitted object. They work with any estimator once its output is pulled out as a matrix.

This article shows the second layer with the joint graphical lasso (JGL; Danaher, Wang & Witten 2014), then how to give a new method the first layer.

Which functions apply to which output

The method returns Examples ggmtools functions
Precision matrices, one per group JGL (fused or group; pcor_estimate() works on its fits), graphical lasso per group, spikeyglass, inverse covariance precision_to_pcor(), threshold_to_adjacency(), kl_divergence(), relative_frobenius(), ggm_bic() (tuning), then everything below
Partial correlations, as matrices or upper-triangle vectors multiGGM pcor_estimate(), DiNGO upper_tri_to_matrix(), diff_edge_table(), threshold_to_adjacency()
Edge scores (higher = more likely an edge or a difference) |partial correlation|, random-forest importance (JRF), D-trace |Δ|, test statistics roc_auc(), pr_auc(), confusion_at_threshold(), topk_overlap()
Posterior edge probabilities multiGGM (MRF priors and mGHS), spikeyglass pip_table() bayes_fdr(), and the score functions above
Permutation or bootstrap null scores any method refitted on permuted labels pooled_perm_pvalues()
Estimated graphs (0/1) any thresholded or selected graph confusion_at_threshold(), diff_adjacency()

Example: the joint graphical lasso

The JGL package was archived on CRAN in July 2025; install it from the CRAN archive or with remotes::install_github("cran/JGL"). It returns a list whose theta element holds one precision matrix per group. Tune the two penalties with ggm_bic(), the BIC used with JGL in the Koyejo lab code (smaller is better):

library(ggmtools)
library(JGL)

grid <- expand.grid(lambda1 = c(0.05, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3),
                    lambda2 = c(0.01, 0.05, 0.1))
grid$bic <- apply(grid, 1, function(g) {
  fit <- JGL(brca_pi3k, penalty = "fused", lambda1 = g[["lambda1"]],
             lambda2 = g[["lambda2"]], return.whole.theta = TRUE)
  ggm_bic(brca_pi3k, fit$theta)
})
best <- grid[which.min(grid$bic), ]
best
#>   lambda1 lambda2      bic
#> 2     0.1    0.01 29.43266

Refit at the chosen penalties. ggmtools has a pcor_estimate() method for JGL fits, which converts each precision matrix with precision_to_pcor(). JGL does not store group names, so pass them, and fit with return.whole.theta = TRUE so that every variable is kept:

fit <- JGL(brca_pi3k, penalty = "fused", lambda1 = best$lambda1,
           lambda2 = best$lambda2, return.whole.theta = TRUE)
genes <- colnames(brca_pi3k$Normal)
pcor <- pcor_estimate(fit, groupnames = names(brca_pi3k))

# Number of edges in each group's graph
sapply(fit$theta, function(theta) sum(threshold_to_adjacency(theta, 1e-8)) / 2)
#> [1] 123 149

The fused penalty sets many differences to exactly 0. diff_edge_table() lists the rest in the shared edge-table format:

d <- diff_edge_table(pcor$Normal, pcor$Tumor, threshold = 1e-8, varnames = genes)
nrow(d)
#> [1] 201
head(d[order(-abs(d$diff)), ])
#>      i  j  node1   node2      est_g1     est_g2       diff
#> 7    3  6   AKT2 MAPKAP1  0.38552727  0.0000000  0.3855273
#> 90   9 19   PDK1  INPP4B -0.04251113 -0.3683474  0.3258362
#> 80   8 18   MTOR  DEPDC5  0.02470883  0.3490456 -0.3243367
#> 107  2 21 AKT1S1   NPRL3  0.29674004  0.0000000  0.2967400
#> 169 17 26  RPTOR   STK11  0.29551205  0.0000000  0.2955121
#> 180 10 27 PIK3CA    TSC1  0.27580379  0.0000000  0.2758038

Do JGL and the unregularized estimate agree on which edges change most? JGL ties every edge it fuses at a difference of exactly 0, so topk_overlap() counts those ties fairly instead of by edge position:

pcor_inv <- lapply(brca_pi3k, function(x) precision_to_pcor(solve(cov(x))))
k <- c(10, 25, 50, 100, 200)
data.frame(k = k,
           overlap = topk_overlap(abs(pcor$Normal - pcor$Tumor),
                                  abs(pcor_inv$Normal - pcor_inv$Tumor), k))
#>     k overlap
#> 1  10       3
#> 2  25       4
#> 3  50      15
#> 4 100      35
#> 5 200     110

In a simulation, where the true graphs are known, the same estimates go straight into roc_auc(), pr_auc() and confusion_at_threshold(), with abs(pcor$Normal) (or threshold_to_adjacency(fit$theta[[1]], 1e-8)) as the score and the true adjacency matrix as the truth.

Example: the multiple graphical horseshoe (mGHS)

mGHS (Busatto & Stingo 2025) is fitted in multiGGM with multiggm_mcmc(method = "mghs"). The fit is a multiGGM fit, so the ggmtools generics work directly. The horseshoe prior has no point mass at zero, so multiGGM defines the edge probability from the shrinkage weights, P(wk,ij>0.5)P(w_{k,ij} > 0.5) with w=λ2/(1+λ2)w = \lambda^2 / (1 + \lambda^2); see the multiGGM documentation.

library(multiGGM)
fit <- multiggm_mcmc(data_list = brca_pi3k, method = "mghs")

pips <- pip_table(fit)       # long table: i, j, node1, node2, group, pip
pcor <- pcor_estimate(fit)   # list of partial-correlation matrices

normal <- pips[pips$group == "Normal", ]
normal$selected <- bayes_fdr(normal$pip, alpha = 0.05)

Giving a new method the generics

pip_table() and pcor_estimate() form a common interface. Supporting a new method means writing an adapter: S3 methods that convert its fitted object into the shared output. ggmtools ships the adapter for JGL fits (class "jgl"), and it is a template for others. Here it is for a hypothetical method whose fits have class "mymethod" and store a list of precision matrices in fit$precision:

pcor_estimate.mymethod <- function(fit, varnames = NULL, groupnames = NULL, ...) {
  out <- lapply(fit$precision, precision_to_pcor)
  p <- nrow(out[[1]])
  varnames <- if (!is.null(varnames)) varnames else
    if (!is.null(rownames(out[[1]]))) rownames(out[[1]]) else paste0("V", seq_len(p))
  out <- lapply(out, function(m) { dimnames(m) <- list(varnames, varnames); m })
  names(out) <- if (!is.null(groupnames)) groupnames else
    paste0("Group_", seq_along(out))
  out
}

In a script, defining the function is enough for dispatch. In a package, register it with S3method(ggmtools::pcor_estimate, mymethod) in the NAMESPACE (with roxygen: @exportS3Method ggmtools::pcor_estimate). A method that returns posterior probabilities can build its pip_table() output with as_pip_table().

References

  • Busatto, C. & Stingo, F.C. (2025). Inference of multiple high-dimensional networks with the Graphical Horseshoe prior. Journal of Computational and Graphical Statistics. doi:10.1080/10618600.2024.2435480
  • Danaher, P., Wang, P. & Witten, D.M. (2014). The joint graphical lasso for inverse covariance estimation across multiple classes. Journal of the Royal Statistical Society: Series B, 76(2), 373-397.
